ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Boris has a big box of building bricks. Each brick is $1 \mathrm{~cm}$ long, $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ wide and $3 \mathrm{~cm}$ high. What is the smallest number of bricks he would need to build a cube?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Each brick has dimensions 1 cm by 2 cm by 3 cm, so one brick has volume 1×2×3 = 6 cm^3. Suppose the cube has side length s cm. Since the cube is built from bricks with integer-centimeter edges, take s to be an integer. The cube volume is s^3, so the number of bricks would be s^3/6. For this to be an integer, s^3 must be divisible by 6. That means s^3 is divisible by both 2 and 3, so s itself must be divisible by both 2 and 3. Therefore the smallest possible integer side length is s = 6. A 6 cm by 6 cm by 6 cm cube has volume 216 cm^3, and 216/6 = 36 bricks are needed. This is achievable by arranging the bricks in a regular grid, for example with the 1 cm, 2 cm, and 3 cm sides aligned along the cube dimensions.

method.method_draft: Use the least-common-multiple packing construction directly. From the text, the brick edge lengths are 1, 2, and 3 cm. To make a cube by stacking congruent bricks in aligned layers, choose the smallest cube side length that is compatible with all three brick dimensions: lcm(1,2,3)=6 cm. Then count how many bricks fit along each direction if the 3 cm side of a brick goes along one cube edge, the 2 cm side along another, and the 1 cm side along the third: 6/3=2, 6/2=3, and 6/1=6. Thus the cube uses 2×3×6=36 bricks. Check that no smaller aligned cube side can work because it would fail to be a common multiple of 1, 2, and 3.
